title: Larkya La Crossing Day: Hour by Hour
meta_description: Larkya La pass day on the Manaslu Circuit: timings from Dharamsala, height gain, snow, what to carry, altitude sickness signs and the descent to Bimthang.
summary: The Larkya La day runs from Dharamsala (≈ 4,460 m) over the 5,106 m pass to Bimthang (≈ 3,590 m): 15 to 16 km and 8 to 10 hours, about 650 m up and 1,500 m down. Leave by 4 or 5 am, carry 2 litres of water, warm layers and microspikes in snow season, and turn back if altitude symptoms appear.

sections.heading: The day in numbers
paras: Every Manaslu Circuit trek builds towards one day: the crossing of Larkya La. Wikipedia and Nepal maps give the pass as 5,106 m, though many agencies quote 5,160 m. What matters more than the exact figure is the shape of the day: a gradual climb in the cold and dark, a short stop at the top and a long, steep descent. The timeline below is typical for a fit group in October.

sections.heading: Acclimatisation in the days before
paras: The crossing is only as good as the days that lead up to it. A sensible itinerary sleeps two nights at Samagaun (3,530 m), one or two at Samdo (3,875 m) and one at Dharamsala (≈ 4,460 m). That keeps each night's gain in sleeping height to roughly 350–600 m above 3,000 m, with the Samagaun rest day as a buffer. Rushed itineraries that skip the second night in Samagaun put most people at a real disadvantage on the pass.

Use the rest days actively. From Samagaun, a hike to Pungyen Gompa at about 4,000 m, or part of the way towards Manaslu Base Camp, followed by a night back in the village, follows the climb-high, sleep-low principle. At Samdo, a walk up the ridge above the village to about 4,200 m does the same. Many trekkers ask their doctor about acetazolamide (Diamox) before the trip; it can help acclimatisation but does not replace a sensible schedule.
list: Night 1 at Samagaun, 3,530 m: arrive from Lho after a 3–4 hour walk
Night 2 at Samagaun: rest-day hike to about 4,000 m or higher
Night 3 at Samdo, 3,875 m: a 3–4 hour walk with about 350 m of gain
Night 4 at Samdo (optional): side hike to about 4,200 m
Night 5 at Dharamsala, ≈ 4,460 m: 3.5–4 hours from Samdo, arrive by lunch

sections.heading: The night before at Dharamsala
paras: Dharamsala, also called Larkya Phedi, is a cluster of stone lodges and tent platforms in a moraine hollow below the Larkya Glacier. You arrive from Samdo in 3.5 to 4 hours, around lunchtime. Use the afternoon well: a short walk 100 to 200 m up the moraine helps acclimatisation, and so does drinking 3 to 4 litres of water through the day.

Eat a full dinner even if your appetite is low, then lay out tomorrow's clothes, fill water bottles with hot water and put them in your sleeping bag, and check headtorch batteries. Many people sleep lightly at this height. That is normal. A severe headache that does not respond to rest and paracetamol, vomiting or confusion are not, and mean you should descend to Samdo, not attempt the pass.

sections.heading: From darkness to the pass
paras: Your guide decides the start time based on the group's pace and conditions, usually between 3 and 5 am. Early starts give you time to cross before the strong winds and cloud that often arrive late morning, and they mean firmer snow on the descent. The first hour climbs onto the lateral moraine of the Larkya Glacier, then follows a line of cairns over rough ground.

The gradient is rarely steep, but the thin air makes every step slow. Walk at a pace where you can breathe through your nose or speak a few words. Stop briefly every 30 to 40 minutes, drink and eat something small, even if you do not feel like it. Dawn usually comes near the frozen lakes below the pass, lighting the peaks around you. The final hour climbs a broad slope to the prayer flags.

sections.heading: On top of Larkya La
paras: The top is marked by a cairn and long strings of prayer flags. To the west a new range appears: Himlung Himal at 7,126 m, Cheo Himal, Kang Guru and Annapurna II at 7,937 m. Behind you lie the Larkya Glacier and the peaks above Samdo. Put on your warm jacket before taking photographs, because the wind is often fierce, and keep gloves on as much as you can.

Most groups stay 10 to 20 minutes. Take your summit photo, drink from a flask, eat and then move on. The descent ahead is long, and staying high in the cold for too long saps energy and increases the risk of altitude problems.

sections.heading: The descent to Bimthang
paras: Many trekkers find the descent harder than the climb. The western side drops steeply on loose scree, often covered with snow or ice from November to April. Use trekking poles, shorten your steps and keep your weight over your feet. Your guide may fit microspikes, simple slip-on chains, if there is ice. Stay together, and wait on safe ground rather than on the steep slope.

After 2 to 3 hours the gradient eases onto moraine and then grassland, and you can relax. The trail passes the Bimthang Glacier and its meltwater lakes, with Manaslu's west face ahead. Reaching Bimthang in mid afternoon, most people feel a mix of exhaustion and elation. Sleep comes easily at 3,590 m.

sections.heading: Daypack, food and pacing
paras: Porters carry your main bag, so your daypack should hold only what you need for the day. Keep it under 6 to 7 kg.

On the pass day you burn far more energy than you can eat, so the aim is to keep topping up. Eat a proper breakfast of porridge, eggs or Tibetan bread even at 3:30 am, and carry snacks you actually like in an outside pocket so you do not have to stop and open your pack. Drink small amounts often. Cold water is hard to face at −10 °C, so hot water or tea in an insulated bottle helps; wrap bottles in a spare sock or carry them upside down so the lids do not freeze.

Guides usually set a slow, steady rhythm, with the lead guide at the front and an assistant guide or porter at the back so that nobody walks alone. If you know you are the slowest member of the group, say so the evening before. It is far safer to leave 30 minutes ahead of the others than to rush to catch up at 5,000 m.
list: Down jacket, windproof shell, fleece and thermal base layers
Warm hat, buff, liner gloves and insulated gloves or mitts
Sunglasses with UV protection, sun cream and lip balm
Headtorch with fresh batteries, plus spares
2 litres of water in insulated bottles or a flask of hot water
Snacks: chocolate, nuts, energy bars, Tibetan bread from breakfast
Trekking poles and microspikes in snow season
Small first-aid kit, personal medicines and a phone or camera kept warm inside your jacket

sections.heading: Weather, snow and when to turn back
paras: Larkya La can be blocked by snow from December to March and briefly in any month, including October and April after storms. Your guide talks to lodge owners and other guides at Samdo and Dharamsala about conditions. If heavy snow or a storm is forecast, the safe choice is to wait a day or turn back to Samagaun, where helicopters can fly you out. Never cross in a whiteout.

Know the signs of altitude illness and be honest with your guide. Mild headache, tiredness and poor sleep are common. Worsening headache, vomiting, loss of coordination, confusion or breathlessness at rest are danger signs of acute mountain sickness, cerebral oedema or pulmonary oedema. The treatment is descent. Your guide carries a pulse oximeter and will make the call if needed.

Before the high point, turning back is simple: Samdo is 3–4 hours down the way you came, and Samagaun has regular helicopter access. Once over the top, the quickest way to lower ground is to keep going down to Bimthang, which is why guides use landmarks such as the frozen lakes as decision points for the group. Helicopter rescue from Dharamsala or Bimthang is possible in clear weather, but afternoon cloud often prevents it.

Your travel insurance must cover emergency helicopter evacuation to at least 5,500 m, and your agency needs the policy number and emergency phone line before the trek starts. Phone coverage is patchy at Dharamsala and on the pass; some lodges have satellite Wi-Fi, and guides usually carry a local SIM that works in parts of the valley. Agree with your guide before you leave who decides to turn back, and accept that decision on the day.

faqs.q: How long does it take to cross Larkya La?
faqs.a: Most trekkers take 8 to 10 hours from Dharamsala to Bimthang: 3 to 5 hours up to the pass at 5,106 m and 4 to 5 hours down. Deep snow or a slow group can stretch it to 11 hours. The distance is about 15 to 16 km.

faqs.q: What time should I start the Larkya La crossing?
faqs.a: Usually between 3 and 5 am. Early starts give time to cross before late-morning wind and cloud and to descend while the snow is firm. Your guide sets the time the evening before based on the group's pace and the latest conditions.

faqs.q: Is Larkya La harder than Thorong La?
faqs.a: Thorong La is about 300 m higher, but many trekkers find Larkya La just as hard because of the long, steep descent and simpler facilities at Dharamsala. Both are non-technical high passes that need good acclimatisation and fitness.

faqs.q: Do I need crampons for Larkya La?
faqs.a: Full crampons are rarely needed for trekkers. From November to April microspikes are very useful on the icy western descent. In heavy snow the pass is usually closed. Your guide will tell you before leaving Samagaun whether to rent microspikes in Kathmandu.

faqs.q: What if I get altitude sickness at Dharamsala?
faqs.a: Do not cross. With mild symptoms you may rest and reassess in the morning. With worsening headache, vomiting, confusion or breathlessness at rest, descend at once to Samdo or Samagaun. Helicopter evacuation can be arranged from Samagaun or, in good weather, from Dharamsala.

faqs.q: Can I hire a horse for Larkya La?
faqs.a: Horses are sometimes available from Samdo or Dharamsala to carry tired trekkers part of the way up, depending on season and conditions. They cannot safely carry riders down the steep western side. Ask your guide in Samagaun; availability is not guaranteed and prices are negotiated locally.

faqs.q: What is the weather like on Larkya La in October?
faqs.a: Usually clear at dawn, with temperatures around −10 to −15 °C at the start and strong, cold wind on the pass. Cloud often builds by late morning. Snow is uncommon in early October but possible after storms. Dress for winter and expect bright sun on the snow.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere to stop between Dharamsala and Bimthang?
faqs.a: There are no lodges or tea shops on the pass itself. Some years a seasonal tent stall operates near the top or on the descent, but do not rely on it. Carry all water and food you need for the day, and plan to reach Bimthang by mid afternoon.

faqs.q: How cold is it at Dharamsala before the pass?
faqs.a: In October nights fall to about −10 °C, and in November to −12 to −15 °C or lower. Rooms are unheated, so sleep in thermals and a hat inside a sleeping bag rated to −15 °C. Keep water bottles, phone and camera batteries inside the bag overnight.
